steps: Every program starts by saying something. We write: print, open bracket, quote, Hello, quote, close bracket. Python shows: Hello!
Python reads from top to bottom. First line: print Knock knock. Second line: print Who is there. So first we see Knock knock, then Who is there.
print can show numbers too. print seven shows seven. print two plus three does the sum first, and shows five.
Put a comma between things to show them together. print, I am, comma, nine, shows: I am nine. Python adds a space between them.
Python is fussy. Print with a capital P is a NameError. And a missing quote, like print, open quote, Hi, with no closing quote, is a SyntaxError.
A hash sign starts a note for humans. hash, say hello to Mia. Then print Hi Mia. Python shows only: Hi Mia. It skips every note.
Single quotes work too. print, single quote Hi, shows Hi. A backslash n inside text starts a new line. print Hi backslash n Bye shows Hi, then Bye on the line below.
Python is a calculator. print two plus three gives five. The star means times: print four star three gives twelve.
The minus sign takes away. print ten minus four gives six. Go below zero and you get a negative: print three minus five gives minus two.
One slash divides and keeps the decimal: seven slash two is three point five. Two slashes keep only the whole number: seven double slash two is three.
The percent sign gives the leftover. seven percent two is one, because three twos make six, and one is left over.
Two stars mean power. two star star three means two times two times two, which is eight.
Python does times before plus. two plus three times four is fourteen. Brackets go first: open bracket, two plus three, close bracket, times four is twenty.

Numbers with a decimal point are called floats. six slash two gives three point zero, a float. round makes it neat: round three point seven gives four. round three point one four one five nine, comma two, keeps two decimals: three point one four.
round three point one four one five nine
Watch the quotes. two plus two is four. But quote two plus quote two is text, so plus glues them: two two.
A string is text, like a book title. We write: title equals quote Python quote. print title shows Python.
The plus sign glues text. quote Book plus quote Club gives BookClub, with no space. Put the space inside the quotes to get Book Club.
len counts the characters. len of book is four: b, o, o, k.
Each letter has a number, starting at zero. word equals cat. word, square bracket zero, gives c, the first letter. Counting starts at zero!
Minus one counts from the end. word equals python. word, square bracket minus one, gives n, the last letter. A colon cuts a slice: word, square bracket zero colon two, gives p y. It stops before two.
Strings have helpers. quote hi dot upper gives HI in capitals. quote HI dot lower gives hi in small letters.
A star repeats text. quote ha, times three, gives ha ha ha. The word in checks if text is inside: quote a in quote cat is True.
You can't glue text and a number. quote Age plus nine is a TypeError. Turn the number into text first with str: quote Age plus str of nine gives Age nine.
An f before the quotes lets you put boxes inside text. name equals Mia. print, f, Hi, curly bracket name, curly bracket. It shows: Hi Mia!
input asks a question and waits, like a letter arriving in your mailbox. We write: name equals input, Name? If you type Mia, then print Hi plus name shows Hi Mia.
Careful! input always gives text. age equals input, Age? You type nine, but age holds the text nine, in quotes. It is not a number yet.
Wrap it in int to get a whole number. age equals int, of input, Age? Now print age plus one shows ten.
For decimal numbers, use float. h equals float, of input, Height? Type one point four, and h holds the number one point four.
You can ask more than once. a equals int, of input, First? b equals int, of input, Second? Then print a plus b. If you type two and three, it shows five.
If you type two and three
What if the answer is not a number? age equals int, of input, Age? If you type the word nine in letters, int can't turn it into a number. That is a ValueError. Type the digit nine instead.
If you type the word nine
Use the answer in a reply. name equals input, Name? Then print, f, Nice to meet you, name. If you type Mia, it says: Nice to meet you, Mia!
Some questions have only two answers, like a lamp: on or off. lamp underscore on equals True. Python calls them True and False. print five greater than three shows True.
Two equal signs ask: are these the same? three equals equals three is True. Exclamation equals means not equal: three not equal four is True. Remember: one equal stores, two equals compare.
Less than and greater than compare sizes. seven less than ten is True. Greater or equal: five greater or equal five is also True.
You can compare text too. quote cat equals equals quote cat is True. But capital Cat equals equals small cat is False. Capitals count!
and is True only when both sides are True. True and True gives True. True and False gives False.
or needs just one side True: True or False gives True. not flips a value: not True gives False.
You can keep an answer in a box. age equals nine. is underscore kid equals age less than thirteen. So is kid holds True.
if lets your program decide. We write: if raining, colon. Then, indented: print Umbrella. It runs only when raining is True.
else means otherwise. if key equals equals gold: print Gate opens. else: print Gate stays shut. Only one of them runs.
elif adds more choices. if age less than six. elif age less than thirteen. else. Python checks from the top, and runs only the first one that is True.
Indenting shows what belongs inside. if happy, colon. Four spaces, print Yay. print Done has no spaces, so it always runs.
Combine checks with and. if sunny and warm: print Beach day. Both must be True.
or runs when either check is True. if day equals equals Sat, or day equals equals Sun: print Weekend. One True is enough.
runs only if both are True
You can put an if inside another if. if hungry, colon. Indented: if has food, colon. Indented again: print Eat. It runs only if both are True.
Let's check a password. word equals input, Password? if word equals equals open sesame: print Welcome.
A loop repeats steps for you, like climbing stairs. for step in range three, colon. Indented: print Climb. It runs three times.
range counts for you, starting at zero. for n in range three: print n. It shows zero, one, two. Three numbers, but no three!
range can start anywhere and jump. range one comma ten comma two starts at one, stops before ten, and jumps by two: one, three, five, seven, nine.
A loop can walk through text, one letter at a time. for ch in quote hey: print ch. It shows h, e, y.
A loop can add things up. total equals zero. for n in range one comma four: total plus equals n. One plus two plus three, so total is six.
for n in range one comma four
while keeps going as long as it is True. steps equals zero. while steps less than three: steps equals steps plus one. When steps reaches three, it stops.
break jumps out of a loop early. for n in range ten: if n equals equals three: break. The loop stops at three.
continue skips the rest of this turn and moves on. for n in range four: if n equals equals two: continue. Then print n. It shows zero, one, three. Two was skipped.
add a break to get out
Careful! while True, colon, never stops on its own. It will print Again, again and again, forever. Always add a break to get out.
Challenge time! The porch-light moth is waiting. hour equals int, of input, Hour? If you type twenty, dark equals hour greater than eighteen, so dark is True.
Now decide. if dark: light equals on. else: light equals off.
To scare the moth away, for blink in range three: print Blink. The light blinks three times.
Finally, say goodnight. name equals input, Name? print, f, Goodnight, name. You used everything from the ground floor!
A variable is a labelled box. We write: pens equals three. Now the box called pens holds three. print pens shows what is inside: three.
Boxes can change. pens equals three, then pens equals five. Now pens holds five, and the three is gone.
You can use a box in maths. pens is five, so total equals pens plus two. total is seven.
You can fill two boxes in one line. a comma b equals one comma two puts one in a, and two in b. To swap them, write a comma b equals b comma a. Now a is two, and b is one.
A box can hold text, a number, or True and False. name equals Mia, in quotes. age equals nine. happy equals True.
Names use letters, numbers and underscores, like my underscore pens. A name can't start with a number, so two pens is a SyntaxError. And capitals matter: Pens and pens are two different boxes.
To add to a box, there is a shortcut. score equals ten. score plus equals five. Now score is fifteen. It is the same as score equals score plus five.
type tells you what kind of value is in a box. type of nine says int, a whole number. type of quote nine says str, a string of text.
a list keeps things in order
A list keeps many things in one row, like beams laid across a floor. beams equals, square bracket, oak, pine, ash. A list keeps them in order. print beams shows all three, inside square brackets.
A list keeps them in order
Each item has a position, starting at zero, just like letters in a string. beams, square bracket zero, gives oak. beams, square bracket minus one, gives the last one: ash.
len counts the items: len of beams is three. The word in checks if something is there: quote oak in beams is True.
Lists can change, unlike strings. beams, square bracket one, equals elm. Now print beams shows oak, elm, ash. The pine was swapped out.
append adds to the end. beams dot append fir puts fir after ash. insert puts an item at a position: beams dot insert, zero, yew, puts yew first.
There are three ways to take items out. beams dot remove ash removes it by name. beams dot pop takes the last one off the end. And del beams, square bracket zero, removes by position.
A slice takes part of a list. beams equals oak, pine, ash, fir. beams, square bracket one colon three, gives pine and ash. It stops before three, like string slices.
beams, square bracket one colon three

A list can hold any kind of value. mix equals three, quote hi, and True. Numbers, text and True or False, all together. An empty list is just two square brackets: empty equals square brackets. Its len is zero.
A for loop walks through a list, one item at a time. pets equals cat, dog, fish. for p in pets, colon. Indented: print p. It shows cat, then dog, then fish.
Need the position too? for i in range of len of pets. Then print i and pets, square bracket i. It shows zero cat, one dog, two fish.
for i in range of len
Python has helpers for lists of numbers. scores equals seven, three, nine. sum of scores adds them up: nineteen. min gives the smallest and max gives the biggest: three and nine.

scores dot sort puts the list in order: three, seven, nine. sorted gives you a new sorted list, and reverse equals True puts the biggest first: nine, seven, three. Remember: sort changes the list itself.
index finds where an item is: pets dot index dog gives one. count says how many times something appears: in one, two, two, three, the count of two is two.
the count of two is two

Careful! a equals one, two. Then b equals a. That does not copy the list: b is a second name for the same list. So b dot append three changes a too! To copy, write c equals a, square bracket, colon. That makes a real copy.
pick the row, then the column

A list can hold other lists, like rows of floorboards. floor equals one, two, and three, four. Pick the row first, then the column. floor, square bracket one, square bracket zero, is row one, column zero: three.
A list can hold other lists

A stack is like a pile of plates. stack dot append adds to the top, and stack dot pop takes from the top: last in, first out. A queue is like a line at the shop. queue dot append joins the end, and queue dot pop zero serves the front: first in, first out.
Build a list with a loop
You can build a list step by step. squares equals an empty list. for n in range four: squares dot append, n times n. Now squares is zero, one, four, nine.

A tuple keeps a few values locked together, like the spot where a post is set in concrete. post equals, round bracket, zero comma four. Tuples use round brackets. print post shows zero, four, in round brackets.
You read a tuple just like a list. post, square bracket zero, gives zero. len of post is two.
But a tuple can never change. post, square bracket zero, equals nine, is a TypeError. Once a tuple is made, it stays the same.
post, square bracket zero, equals nine
A tuple with one item needs a comma. one equals, round bracket, five, comma. That is a tuple. Without the comma, num equals, round bracket five, is just the number five.
Unpacking takes the values out into boxes. x comma y equals post. Now x is zero and y is four.
b, a makes a tuple, then unpacks it
Remember the swap from Variables? a comma b equals one comma two. Then a comma b equals b comma a. The right side makes a tuple, then Python unpacks it into a and b.
a comma b equals one comma two
Then a comma b equals b comma a
The right side makes a tuple
Which should you use? If it will change, like a shopping list, use a list. If it is fixed for ever, use a tuple. The days of the week never change: days equals Mon, Tue, Wed, in round brackets.
If it is fixed for ever
A list can hold tuples. posts equals a list of three spots. for x comma y in posts: print x plus y. Each turn unpacks one tuple. It shows zero, four, four.
for x comma y in posts
A set is a bag of things with no repeats, like the walls of a room. walls equals, curly bracket, north, south. Sets use curly brackets. print len of walls shows two.
Put repeats in, and they vanish. nums equals one, one, two, two, three. print nums shows just one, two, three.
A set has no order, so there is no first item. walls, square bracket zero, is a TypeError. A set has no positions.
Sets can grow and shrink. walls dot add east puts east in. Add east again, and nothing happens: it is already there. walls dot discard west takes west out. If west is not there, there is no error.
in checks if something is in the set. quote north in walls is True. Sets can check this very fast, even when they are huge.
Sets can be combined. a equals one, two, three, and b equals two, three, four. The bar joins them: a bar b is one, two, three, four. The and sign gives the overlap: a and b is two, three.
a and b is two, three
in a, but not in b
The minus sign finds what is missing. a minus b is just one: it is in a, but not in b.
it is in a, but not in b
A quick trick: names equals Mia, Ali, Mia. set of names removes the repeat, leaving Mia and Ali. One catch: an empty set is written set, with round brackets. Empty curly brackets make a dictionary.

A dictionary stores values under names, like a key rack where every hook has a label. rooms equals, curly bracket, bed colon bunk, bath colon tub. The name on the left is the key, and the thing on the right is its value.
use the key, not a position
To look something up, use its key in square brackets. rooms, square bracket bath, gives tub. You use the key, not a position.
Ask for a key that is not there, and you get an error. rooms, square bracket attic, is a KeyError. get is safer: rooms dot get attic, comma none, gives none instead.
Adding is easy. rooms, square bracket study, equals desk. study is a new key, so it is added. rooms, square bracket bed, equals sofa bed. bed was already there, so its value is changed.
To remove a key, write del rooms, square bracket study. rooms dot pop bath removes bath too, and gives back its value: tub.
dot items gives you every key with its value. for room comma thing in rooms dot items: print room and thing. It shows bed bunk, then bath tub.
in looks at the keys, not the values. quote bed in rooms is True. But quote bunk in rooms is False, because bunk is a value.
A value can be a whole list. rooms equals bed, colon, a list of bunk and lamp. rooms, square bracket bed, square bracket one, gives lamp.
rooms, square bracket bed, square bracket one
Last, some helpers. len of rooms counts the keys. rooms dot keys gives all the keys, and rooms dot values gives all the values. Wrap them in list to see them.

Like tuples, strings can never change. word equals Jam. word, square bracket zero, equals H, is a TypeError. Instead, build a new string: word equals H plus word, square bracket one colon. Now word is Ham.
word, square bracket zero, equals H
replace swaps one piece of text for another. quote cat, dot replace, c, b, gives bat. It gives you a new string, and the old one stays the same.
It gives you a new string
split cuts text into a list of words. quote red green blue, dot split, gives a list: red, green, blue. join does the opposite. quote dash, dot join, a, b, c, glues them with dashes: a dash b dash c.
strip removes spaces from both ends. quote, space space hi space space, dot strip, gives just hi. It's great for cleaning up what people type.
Strings can search themselves. s equals hello. s dot find l gives two, the first place l appears. s dot count l is also two: there are two of them.
These checks tell you what kind of text it is. quote forty two, dot isdigit, is True: all digits. quote hi, dot isalpha, is True: all letters. Check with isdigit before you use int.
A slice can take steps. s equals python. s, square bracket, colon colon two, takes every second letter: p, t, o. And colon colon minus one walks backwards: it reverses the word.
s, square bracket, colon colon two

f-strings can format numbers. price equals three point five. f, curly bracket price, colon, point two f, shows three point five zero: two decimal places, like money. And colon, greater than three, pads seven to three spaces wide.
Older code uses dot format. quote Hi, curly brackets, dot format Mia, fills the brackets: Hi Mia! You'll see it in older code, but f-strings are newer and shorter.
A function is a recipe you write once and use again and again. def hello, colon. Indented: print Hi. Nothing happens yet! Then hello, with brackets, runs it and shows Hi.
A parameter is an ingredient you hand in. def hello, name, colon. print Hi, name. hello Mia puts Mia into name, and shows Hi Mia.
return hands a value back. def double, n. return n times two. x equals double five, so x is ten.
→ shows HI, but x is None
print and return are different. def shout, w. print w dot upper. x equals shout hi shows HI on the screen, but x is None, because shout never returned anything.
A function can take several parameters, in order. def area, w comma h. return w times h. area three, four: w is three, h is four, so it gives twelve.
Functions can call other functions. def floor, n. return area n, n. floor five calls area five, five, which gives twenty five.
A docstring explains what a function does. Under def area, write it in three quotes: Width times height. The return comes after it. Then help of area shows that note.
Why bother? Write it once. Use it anywhere. And if there is a bug, you fix it in one place, not ten.
you fix it in one place

A parameter can have a default, like the dial on a toaster. def toast, n, level equals three. It prints the slices and the level. toast two leaves level out, so it uses three: two slices at level three.
A parameter can have a default
def toast, n, level equals three
names, so order does not matter
You can name the arguments. toast, level equals five, n equals two, gives two slices at level five. With names, the order does not matter.
Mix them like this: toast two, level equals five. That's fine: plain arguments come first. But toast, level equals five, then two, is a SyntaxError.
A function can return two things at once. def size. return three comma four. That's a tuple! w comma h equals size unpacks it: w is three, h is four.
w is three, h is four
A star lets a function take any number of values. def total, star nums. return sum of nums. total one, two, three gives six. nums arrives as a tuple.
Two stars collect named values into a dictionary. def order, star star items. print items. order, tea equals two, cake equals one, shows a dictionary: tea two, cake one.
A box made inside a function belongs to that function. x equals one. def f. Inside, x equals five: a new local x. After f runs, print x still shows one. The outside x never changed.
global, and why to avoid it
The word global lets a function change an outside box. def f. global x. x equals five. Now the outside x changes. It works, but it makes code hard to follow, so return a value instead.
A function can even call itself. def countdown, n. if n equals equals zero, return. print n. Then countdown n minus one. countdown three shows three, two, one, then stops at zero.
A function can even call itself
When Python gets stuck, it names the problem. int of hi is a ValueError: not a number. Text plus a number is a TypeError: the wrong kinds. Five divided by zero is a ZeroDivisionError.
IndexError: list index out of range
the last line says what went wrong
The message tells you what went wrong. nums equals one, two. nums, square bracket five. Python says: IndexError, list index out of range. Always read the last line first.
try lets your program catch a problem instead of crashing. try, colon. n equals int of hi. That fails, so Python jumps to except, colon, and prints Not a number. The program keeps going!
It's better to name the error you expect. except ValueError, colon, only catches ValueError. Any other bug still shows up, so you can find it.
Any other bug still shows up
You can catch different errors in different ways. try: x equals ten divided by int of s. except ValueError: print Type a number. except ZeroDivisionError: print Not zero.
Put it together with a loop. while True: try: age equals int of input, Age? If that works, break out of the loop. except ValueError: print Digits please, and ask again.
Be careful with a bare except, colon. It catches everything, even your own typos, and hides them. Name the error you expect instead.
read gives the whole file as text
A file keeps your data after the program ends, like a notebook in the attic. f equals open notes dot t x t. text equals f dot read: the whole file as one string. Then f dot close, to put it away.
the whole file as one string
with is the safe way. with open notes as f, colon. Indented: text equals f dot read. When the indented part ends, the file is closed for you, even if something goes wrong.
w wipes the old file first!
To write, open with w. with open notes, comma w, as f. f dot write Hi, backslash n. Careful: w wipes everything that was in the file first!
To add without wiping, open with a, for append. with open notes, comma a, as f. f dot write More. The old lines stay, and More goes on the end.
A for loop reads a file one line at a time. with open notes as f. for line in f: print line dot strip. strip removes the new line at the end. It shows Hi, then More.
import csv does this for whole files
A CSV file stores a table, with commas between the columns. row equals Mia comma nine comma blue. row dot split comma gives a list: Mia, nine, blue. For whole files, import csv does this for you.
Open a file that is not there, and you get an error. open nope dot t x t is a FileNotFoundError. Catch it with except FileNotFoundError, just like the smoke alarm.
Open a file that is not there
or a path to another folder
Where does Python look? open notes dot t x t looks in the same folder as your program. open data slash notes dot t x t looks inside the data folder: that is called a path.
open notes dot t x t
a module is a box of tools
Nobody builds their own hammer. import math opens the maths toolbox. A module is a box of tools someone already made.
Use a tool with a dot. math dot sqrt sixteen gives the square root: four point oh. math dot pi is pi: three point one four one five nine.
Use a tool with a dot
ceil always rounds up: math dot ceil two point one is three. floor always rounds down: math dot floor two point nine is two.
math dot ceil two point one
math dot floor two point nine
Sometimes you only need one tool. from math import sqrt takes it out of the box. Now you can write sqrt twenty five, without math dot. It gives five point oh.
r is a nickname for random
as gives a module a nickname. import random as r. Now r dot randint one, six rolls a dice. r is a nickname for random.
The random module makes surprises. random dot randint one, six gives a whole number from one to six, including six. random dot choice picks one item from a list.
a whole number from one to six
Two more tricks. random dot shuffle cards mixes the list itself, like shuffling a deck. random dot seed one makes the random numbers come out the same every time. That helps when testing.
come out the same every time
Want to see inside a module? dir of math lists every tool in it. help of math dot sqrt explains one tool, using its docstring.
Challenge time! Plan a garden party on your new balcony. names equals an empty list. with open guests dot t x t as f: for line in f: names dot append line dot strip. Now every guest is in the list.
Some names were written twice. guests equals set of names removes the repeats. print len of guests says how many people are really coming.
how many people are really coming
A dictionary says who brings what. food equals Mia, pizza, and Ali, cake. food dot get Sam, comma snacks: Sam is not in it, so Sam brings snacks.
Write a helper to seat everyone. import random. def seat, people. people equals list of people. random dot shuffle people. return people. Every party gets a new seating plan!
Last, ask how many chairs, safely. try: chairs equals int of input, Chairs? except ValueError: chairs equals ten. Whatever they type, the party is ready. You used everything on floor two!
A module is just a Python file. Make a file called tools dot p y. Inside: def hammer, and return bang. Any dot p y file you write is a module.
In another file in the same folder, write import tools. Then tools dot hammer, with brackets, runs your function and gives bang.
from tools import hammer as h
import * hides where names come from
from tools import hammer as h brings in just hammer, with a short name. Now h, with brackets, works. Avoid import star: it pours in every name, and you can't tell where they came from.
from tools import hammer as h
Two ways to look around. dir of tools lists the names inside your module, like hammer. import sys, then sys dot path is the list of folders Python searches when you import something.
runs only when you run this file

Every module has a name. When you run the file itself, its name is dunder main. So, if dunder name equals equals dunder main, colon, print hammer. That line runs only when you run this file, not when another file imports it.
A package is a folder of modules, like a workshop full of toolboxes. The folder workshop holds a file called dunder init dot p y, and a module saws dot p y. Then from workshop import saws.
After an import, you may see a folder called dunder pycache. Python saves ready-to-run copies of your modules there, so they load faster next time. You can leave it alone.

pip is the delivery van: it brings packages other people made. pip install requests downloads one. A file called requirements dot t x t lists what your project needs, like requests, double equals, two point three two.
A virtual environment gives each project its own separate set of packages. python, dash m, venv, dot venv makes one. Now two projects can use different versions without a fight.
Python checks except blocks from the top. Put the specific one first: except ValueError. Then the general one: except Exception. The other way round, the general one would catch everything first.
To catch several kinds the same way, put them in a tuple. except, round bracket, ValueError comma TypeError. One block handles both.
as gives the error a name, so you can look at it. except ValueError as e. print e shows Python's message about what went wrong.
else runs only if nothing went wrong. try: n equals int of s. except ValueError. else: print Got, n.
finally runs whatever happens, error or not, like unclipping your harness at the end. try: climb. finally: unclip harness. Even if climbing goes wrong, the harness is unclipped.
except ArithmeticError catches its children too
Errors form a family tree. Exception is at the top. ArithmeticError is one of its children, and ZeroDivisionError is a child of that. So except ArithmeticError also catches ZeroDivisionError.
raise makes an error on purpose. raise ValueError, too high. Inside an except, you can do something, like log it, then write raise on its own. That passes the same error on up.
then write raise on its own
You can make your own kind of error. class FallError, round bracket Exception, colon, pass. Now raise FallError, Slipped! It works like any other error.
Sometimes one error causes another. except KeyError as e. Then raise SafetyError, no rope, from e. The message shows both errors, so you can see what started it.
Inside the computer, every letter is a number. ord of capital A gives sixty five. In the old ASCII code, capital A is sixty five.
chr goes the other way. chr of ninety seven gives small a. chr of, ord of a, plus one, gives the next letter: b.

ASCII only has English letters. Unicode has a number for every character in every language. ord of e with an accent is two hundred thirty three. ord of the Chinese character for middle is twenty thousand and thirteen.
ord of e with an accent
2 bytes for é, 1 byte for A
To save text in a file, Unicode numbers become bytes. UTF-8 is the usual way. e with an accent, dot encode, gives two bytes. Capital A needs just one byte.
To save text in a file
e with an accent, dot encode
Bytes have a small b in front of the quotes. b, quote hi, is bytes, not text. dot decode turns bytes back into text: hi.
len counts characters in text, but bytes in bytes. len of e accent is one character. len of its encoded bytes is two.
Strings can check their own characters. quote seven, dot isdigit, is True. A space, dot isspace, is True too. There are more: isupper, islower and isalnum.
Python compares text by these numbers. Capital Z less than small a is True, because Z is ninety and small a is ninety seven. Capital letters come first.
Capital Z less than small a
Because capitals come first, sorting can surprise you. sorted of bee, Ant, cat puts Ant first. To ignore capitals, add key equals str dot lower. Now ant, bee and Cat come in alphabet order.
a plan, not a window yet
A class is a blueprint, a plan for making things. class Dormer, colon. Indented: pass, which means nothing inside yet. A blueprint is a plan, not a window yet.
An object is made from it
Call the class like a function to make an object. d equals Dormer, with brackets. Now d is one real dormer, made from the blueprint.
Now d is one real dormer
dunder init runs every time a new object is made. Inside class Dormer: def dunder init, self, colour. Then self dot colour equals colour.
self is the object being made or used. d equals Dormer, blue. So print d dot colour shows blue. While dunder init ran, self was d.
Attributes are an object's own values. d dot colour equals red changes it. d dot width equals two adds a new one. Each object keeps its own.
